query: How should we pre‑specify primary vs secondary outcomes and multiplicity adjustments to avoid fishing and facilitate policy uptake?

response.query: How should we pre‑specify primary vs secondary outcomes and multiplicity adjustments to avoid fishing and facilitate policy uptake?
response.answer: Pre-specify primary outcomes clearly in the study protocol; use statistical methods for multiplicity adjustments; avoid post-hoc analyses to prevent fishing.

results.title: Pesticide-Induced Diseases: Body Burden
results.content: In this study, concentrations of six parent NEOs (p-NEOs) and N-desmethyl-acetamiprid (N-dm-ACE) were measured in urine and whole blood samples from infants, in addition to breast milk, infant formula, and tap water collected in South China. Presently, the potential health risks of neonicotinoid insecticides (neonics) are now receiving much attention, but no data regarding the exposure of infants to neonics via human breast milk intake have been reported. * Organochlorine pesticides (OCPs) and polychlorinated biphenyls (PCBs) in human breast milk and associated health risks to nursing infants in Northern Tanzania. Ninety-five healthy mother-infant couples attending Mount Meru Regional Referral Hospital (MMRRH), Arusha, Tanzania, were assessed for associations between maternal/infant characteristics, i.e. mother's age, BMI, gestational weight gain, occupation, residence and fetal growth parameters and breast milk levels of OCPs, such as dichlorodiphenyltrichloroethane (DDT) and its metabolites, dieldrin and PCBs. p,p'-DDE and p,p'-DDT were detected in 100% and 75% of the breast milk samples, respectively, and ranged between 24 and 2400ng/g lipid weight (lw) and.

results.title: Findings: OECD Development Co-operation Peer Reviews
results.content: **Global crises and shifting geopolitics place increasing demands on Switzerland’s international co-operation.** Russia’s war of aggression against Ukraine, other violent conflicts, climate change, and the lingering impacts of the COVID-19 pandemic are exacerbating poverty, inequality, and food insecurity, and undermining governance in many partner countries [(OECD, 2024[1])](/en/publications/oecd-development-co-operation-peer-reviews-switzerland-2025_b83b7007-en/full-report/findings_0294d85e.html#OEC243_dda1a432fd). Despite solid public support for international co-operation [(ETH Zürich, 2024[3])](/en/publications/oecd-development-co-operation-peer-reviews-switzerland-2025_b83b7007-en/full-report/findings_0294d85e.html#ETH24_dda1a432fd), taking effect from 2025, parliament decided to cut the budget – apart from humanitarian aid – to create more fiscal space for defence expenditures. As highlighted in Switzerland's International Cooperation Strategy 2021-2024 [(FDFA, 2020[12])](/en/publications/oecd-development-co-operation-peer-reviews-switzerland-2025_b83b7007-en/full-report/findings_0294d85e.html#Fed20_dda1a432fd), a stable and investment-friendly business environment is key to Switzerland’s prosperity. The Foreign Policy Strategy serves as the overarching guideline [(State Secretariat for Economic Affairs, 2021[13])](/en/publications/oecd-development-co-operation-peer-reviews-switzerland-2025_b83b7007-en/full-report/findings_0294d85e.html#Sta21_dda1a432fd), concretised through five geographic and four thematic strategies, including the International Cooperation Strategy [(FDFA, 2020[12])](/en/publications/oecd-development-co-operation-peer-reviews-switzerland-2025_b83b7007-en/full-report/findings_0294d85e.html#Fed20_dda1a432fd). The 1976 law and ordinance on international co-operation provide the legal framework for the strategy [(Federal Assembly of the Swiss Conferederation, 1976[14])](/en/publications/oecd-development-co-operation-peer-reviews-switzerland-2025_b83b7007-en/full-report/findings_0294d85e.html#Ass76_dda1a432fd).
